nodes.question: What substance was tested for its removal potential in the experimental runs?
nodes.answer: DEET was tested for its removal potential in the experimental runs.
nodes.paragraph: Two distinct experimental runs were conducted to evaluate removal potential: control runs (without DEET) and test runs (with DEET). The test runs included T1 (5 mg/L), T2 (10 mg/L), and T3 (25 mg/L), all performed in a 250- mL Erlenmeyer flask containing 100 mL of BG-11 algal medium inoculated with Chlorella vulgaris during the growth phase. experimental configuration. Removal studies were con - ducted in an algal growth chamber equipped with an incubating orbital shaker operating at 120 rpm and a light intensity of 2000 Ix, following a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle at a temperature of 30 1 C until the algal species reached the death phase of their growth cycle. Determination of algal growth and pigments A light microscope with total magnification of 40 and a Neubauer hemocytometer was used to evaluate algal growth based on the cell density under both test and con - trol conditions. nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: How many species of halophilic PPB were highlighted as capable of producing three or more chemicals simultaneously?
nodes.answer: The study highlighted 22 species capable of producing three or more chemicals simultaneously.
nodes.paragraph: Through a compre- hensive literature review, we compiled a list of halo- philic PPB and mined their genomes for genes linked to CO /CO utilization as carbon sources. Further genomic search revealed genes encoding enzymes for ectoine/hydroxyectoine, proline, ubiquinone, and carotenoids (lycopene, -carotene, spirilloxanthin, and spheroidene). We identified 276 genomes of PPB with the genomic potential to valorise CO /CO into health-promoting ingredients, highlighting 22 spe- cies capable of producing three or more chemicals simultaneously. These findings highlight the untapped potential of halophilic PPB as bio-platforms for sus- tainable pharmaceutical production.Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https:// doi. org/ 10. 1007/ s11157- 25- 9722-w . nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean water and sanitation|Drinking water standards and regulations|Disinfection byproduct regulations_qna_002
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: How many chemicals have been estimated as likely POPs according to the Stockholm Convention POP criteria?
nodes.answer: Approximately 590 chemicals are estimated to be likely POPs.
nodes.paragraph: In many industrial countries, chemical produc tion wastes including POPs were largely landfilled or dumped until the 1970s and even 1980s [87, 94, 97, 115, 220, 296, 348, 362, 378]. In low and middle income countries, such production waste is still disposed mostly in dumpsites and landfills due to the limited or absence of destruction capacity [4 , 61, 362, 363]. During the past 60 years brominated, chlorinated and fluorinated POPs and other PBTs have been increas ingly produced [257, 283] and used in consumer goods [39, 40, 112, 121, 273, 316]. An assessment of registered chemicals estimated that approximately 590 of these chemicals are likely POPs considering the Stockholm Convention POP criteria [257]. As products containing these POPs/PBTs reach the end of life, these chemi cals end up in the waste stream [307, 308, 316]. Most low and middle income countries have very limited adequate recycling, treatment, and destruction capac ity, and many countries have relied heavily on landfills and dumps [12, 13, 362, 363].
